items.title: The Five Dynasties (1206–1526) & Ghurid Foundation
items.body:
### The Delhi Sultanate

**In one line:** The Delhi Sultanate was the first big Muslim-ruled kingdom based at Delhi, run by five Turkish/Afghan dynasties one after another from 1206 to 1526.

**Why it is asked:** APPSC loves the order of the five dynasties and the three big battles that opened the door to Turkish rule. Define once: a *Sultanate* = a state ruled by a *Sultan* (a Muslim king); a *dynasty* = a family that passes the throne down its own line.

**The story**

- Before Delhi had a Sultan, a ruler from Ghur (in today's Afghanistan), **Muhammad Ghuri**, raided north India. He **lost** the **First Battle of Tarain (1191)** to the Rajput king **Prithviraj Chauhan**, came back, and **won** the **Second Battle of Tarain (1192)** — the turning point.
- Two years later, the **Battle of Chandawar (1194)** crushed **Jaichandra** of Kannauj (the Gahadavala king). Ghuri's general **Bakhtiyar Khalji** then overran **Bihar and Bengal** (defeating **Lakshman Sena**) and destroyed its Buddhist monasteries.
- When Ghuri died in **1206**, his trusted slave-governor **Qutb-ud-din Aibak** stopped taking orders from Ghazni and set himself up as an independent ruler at Delhi. That act **started the Delhi Sultanate**.
- Five families then ruled in turn. The last Sultan, **Ibrahim Lodi**, was killed by **Babur** at the **First Battle of Panipat (1526)**, which ended the Sultanate and began the Mughal Empire.

**Why it matters:** These wars explain *how* a Central-Asian military elite came to rule north India for 300 years — a favourite "cause and effect" theme in both Prelims and Mains.

**Picture it**

| Dynasty | Period | Founder |
|---|---|---|
| Slave / Mamluk | 1206–1290 | Qutb-ud-din Aibak |
| Khalji | 1290–1320 | Jalaluddin Khalji |
| Tughlaq | 1320–1414 | Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq |
| Sayyid | 1414–1451 | Khizr Khan |
| Lodi | 1451–1526 | Bahlol Lodi |

**Terms explained**
- **Mamluk** = a slave soldier who rose to power; the first dynasty is called Slave/Mamluk because its founders were former slaves.
- **Ghurid** = belonging to the Ghur region of Afghanistan, Ghuri's homeland.

**Don't confuse:** The **two Battles of Tarain** — 1191 was Prithviraj's **win**, 1192 was Ghuri's decisive **win**. Chandawar (1194) is a **separate** battle against Jaichandra, not Prithviraj.

**Remember it:** Dynasty order "Slave Kings Take Some Land" = **S**lave, **K**halji, **T**ughlaq, **S**ayyid, **L**odi.

**TL;DR**
- Tarain I (1191) = Prithviraj's win; Tarain II (1192) = Ghuri's decisive win.
- Chandawar (1194) defeated Jaichandra of Kannauj; Tarain + Chandawar founded Turkish rule in north India.
- Sultanate began 1206 (Aibak) and ended 1526 (Babur beat Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat).
- Five dynasties in order: Slave → Khalji → Tughlaq → Sayyid → Lodi.
keyPoints: First Battle of Tarain (1191) = Prithviraj's win; Second Battle of Tarain (1192) = Muhammad Ghuri's decisive victory.
Battle of Chandawar (1194) defeated Jaichandra (Gahadavala) of Kannauj; Tarain + Chandawar founded Turkish rule in North India.
Delhi Sultanate began in 1206 when Qutb-ud-din Aibak declared independence after Ghuri's death.
Five dynasties in order: Slave (1206) → Khalji (1290) → Tughlaq (1320) → Sayyid (1414) → Lodi (1451).
The Sultanate ended at the First Battle of Panipat (1526), Babur defeating Ibrahim Lodi.

items.title: Slave (Mamluk) Dynasty — Aibak to Balban
items.body:
### The Slave (Mamluk) Dynasty, 1206–1290

**In one line:** The first dynasty of the Sultanate, founded by former slave-soldiers, where Aibak started it, Iltutmish truly built it, Razia briefly ruled, and Balban made the throne feared.

**Why it is asked:** Each ruler has one or two "signature" facts the exam tests (who began the Qutb Minar, who issued the tanka, the only woman ruler, who introduced sijda). Define once: *tanka* = the silver coin of the Sultanate; *iqta* = a piece of land whose tax a noble could collect in return for keeping soldiers (explained in the administration note).

**The story**

- **Qutb-ud-din Aibak (1206–1210)** was the first Sultan. He was called **Lakh Baksh** ('giver of lakhs') for his huge gifts to the poor. He **began** the **Qutub Minar** (named in honour of the Sufi saint **Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki**) and built the **Quwwat-ul-Islam** mosque (Delhi) and **Adhai-din-ka-Jhonpra** (Ajmer). His court was at **Lahore**, and he died in a fall while playing polo (*chaugan*).
- **Iltutmish (1211–1236)** was Aibak's slave and son-in-law, and the real builder of the state. He shifted the capital from **Lahore to Delhi**, issued the first proper **silver tanka** and copper **jital**, organised the **iqta** system, and set up the **Turkan-i-Chihalgani** (a Council of Forty loyal Turkish nobles). He completed the Qutub Minar and named his daughter **Razia** as heir.
- **Razia Sultana (1236–1240)** was the **first and only woman** to rule Delhi. Her father Iltutmish nominated her as heir in preference to his sons. She was able, but the Turkish nobles of the **Chihalgani** strongly opposed a woman ruler; she married **Malik Altunia** to win back power, and was defeated and killed.
- **Ghiyasuddin Balban (1266–1287)** ruled by a stern **'blood and iron'** policy. He forced courtiers to perform **sijda** (bowing to the ground) and **paibos** (kissing the Sultan's feet), and called the king **Zill-i-Ilahi** ('Shadow of God'). He broke the power of the **Chihalgani**, crushed the Bengal rebel **Tughril Beg**, and patronised the poet **Amir Khusrau**.

**Why it matters:** This dynasty shows how a shaky new state was turned into a strong monarchy — from Aibak's rough start to Balban's awe-inspiring kingship.

**Terms explained**
- **Chihalgani** = 'the Forty', a group of powerful Turkish nobles; they often decided who became Sultan.
- **Zill-i-Ilahi** = 'Shadow of God', a title to make the king seem semi-divine and above the nobles.

**Don't confuse:** **Aibak** only *began* the Qutub Minar at **Lahore**-based court; **Iltutmish** *completed* it and made **Delhi** the capital. The tanka is Iltutmish's, not Aibak's. The **market price-control system** is **Alauddin Khalji's** reform — not Iltutmish's.

**Remember it:** "Aibak begins, Iltutmish builds, Razia breaks the glass ceiling, Balban terrifies."

**TL;DR**
- Aibak = first Sultan, 'Lakh Baksh', began Qutub Minar; capital at Lahore.
- Iltutmish shifted capital to Delhi, issued the silver tanka, organised iqta and the Chihalgani.
- Razia (1236–1240) = first and only woman ruler of Delhi.
- Balban = 'blood and iron', sijda & paibos, Zill-i-Ilahi; broke the Chihalgani and beat Tughril Beg.
keyPoints: Qutb-ud-din Aibak = first Sultan, 'Lakh Baksh', began Qutub Minar; capital at Lahore.
Iltutmish shifted capital to Delhi, issued the silver tanka, organised the iqta system and the Chihalgani (Council of Forty).
Razia Sultana (1236–1240) was the first and only woman ruler of the Delhi Sultanate.
Balban's 'blood and iron' policy, sijda and paibos, and the Zill-i-Ilahi ideal exalted royal authority.
Balban broke the power of the Chihalgani and crushed the Bengal rebel Tughril Beg.
Aibak began the Qutub Minar in honour of the Sufi saint Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki; Lakh Baksh = giver of lakhs (liberal charity).
Iltutmish nominated Razia in preference to his sons; the Chihalgani nobles opposed her.

items.title: Khalji Dynasty & Alauddin's Reforms
items.body:
### The Khalji Dynasty & Alauddin's Reforms, 1290–1320

**In one line:** The Khaljis widened who could rule beyond a narrow Turkish circle, and their greatest Sultan, Alauddin Khalji, conquered widely and ran one of history's strictest price-control systems to fund a huge army.

**Why it is asked:** Alauddin's **conquests**, his **market control** and his **military reforms** are three of the most tested themes in medieval history. Define once: *market/price control* = the state fixing the selling price of goods by law; a *standing army* = full-time soldiers paid by the state, not called up only in war.

**The story**

- **Jalaluddin Khalji** founded the dynasty in **1290** by overthrowing the last Slave (Mamluk) ruler. He made **Kilokhri** his capital and followed a relatively mild, tolerant policy. In **1296** he was murdered by his nephew and son-in-law **Alauddin Khalji** after a rich raid on **Devagiri** — a shift of power called the **'Khalji revolution'** because the throne passed beyond the old Turkish nobility.
- **Alauddin (1296–1316)** conquered the **north**: Gujarat (raided 1299, annexed 1304), **Ranthambore (1301)**, **Chittor (1303)**, **Malwa (1305)**, Siwana (1308) and Jalore (1311), and repeatedly beat back **Mongol** invasions.
- In the **Deccan**, his general **Malik Kafur** led tribute-raids against **Devagiri** (Yadavas), **Warangal** (Kakatiyas), **Dwarasamudra** (Hoysalas) and **Madurai** (Pandyas), bringing huge wealth to Delhi.
- **Market control:** to keep a big army cheaply, he **fixed low prices** for essentials. Delhi had three controlled markets — the grain **mandi**, the cloth-and-general **Sarai Adl**, and one for horses/slaves/cattle — each watched by a **Shahna-i-Mandi** (market superintendent). The **Diwan-i-Riyasat** registered every trader, and spies (**Barid** and **munhiyans**) reported daily; hoarders were punished.
- **Military reform:** he was the first to keep a **large cash-paid standing army**, using **Dagh** (branding horses with a state mark) and **Chehra** (a written description of each soldier) to stop fraud at muster.

**Why it matters:** The link between the two reforms is the exam's favourite point — **cheap fixed prices made fixed cash salaries affordable**, so a giant army became possible. The system worked while Alauddin lived but collapsed after 1316 because it rested on fear, not markets.

**Terms explained**
- **Mandi** = the grain market; **Sarai Adl** = the cloth and general-goods market.
- **Dagh** = branding of horses; **Chehra** = the soldier's descriptive roll — both stopped officers from faking their troop numbers.

**Don't confuse:** **Dagh/Chehra** and the cash army are **Alauddin's**, while the **iqta and the tanka** belong to **Iltutmish**. Token (copper) currency is **Muhammad-bin-Tughlaq's**, not Alauddin's.

**Remember it:** "Dagh brands the horse, Chehra describes the man."

**TL;DR**
- Jalaluddin founded the Khaljis (1290); Alauddin seized power in 1296 (the 'Khalji revolution').
- North conquests: Gujarat, Ranthambore (1301), Chittor (1303), Malwa (1305); Mongols repelled.
- Malik Kafur's Deccan raids: Devagiri (Yadava), Warangal (Kakatiya), Dwarasamudra (Hoysala), Madurai (Pandya).
- Market control (mandi, Sarai Adl, Shahna-i-Mandi, Diwan-i-Riyasat) funded the first cash-paid standing army with Dagh & Chehra.
keyPoints: Jalaluddin Khalji founded the dynasty in 1290; Alauddin Khalji seized power in 1296 (the 'Khalji revolution').
Alauddin's North Indian conquests: Gujarat, Ranthambore (1301), Chittor (1303), Malwa (1305); repelled the Mongols.
Malik Kafur's Deccan raids hit Devagiri (Yadava), Warangal (Kakatiya), Dwarasamudra (Hoysala) and Madurai (Pandya).
Market control: fixed low prices, markets (mandi, Sarai Adl), Shahna-i-Mandi supervisor and Diwan-i-Riyasat merchant registry.
Alauddin was first to keep a cash-paid standing army with the Dagh (branding) and Chehra (soldier roll) system.

items.title: Tughlaq Dynasty — Experiments, Welfare & Timur
items.body:
### The Tughlaq Dynasty, 1320–1414

**In one line:** The Tughlaqs rose to the Sultanate's largest size, then declined — remembered for Muhammad-bin-Tughlaq's famous 'failed experiments', Firoz Shah's welfare works, and Timur's sack of Delhi.

**Why it is asked:** The four 'experiments' of Muhammad-bin-Tughlaq and the welfare schemes of Firoz Shah are among the most asked Sultanate facts. Define once: *token currency* = coins made of a cheap metal (copper) but ordered to be worth as much as silver; *jizya* = a tax on non-Muslims.

**The story**

- **Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq (1320–1325)** founded the dynasty after defeating the usurper **Khusrau Khan**. He built the massive **Tughlaqabad Fort** and strengthened postal, judicial, irrigation and farming administration.
- **Muhammad-bin-Tughlaq (1325–1351)** is famous for four schemes that were clever in idea but failed in practice: (1) moving the **capital from Delhi to Daulatabad (Devagiri)** and later back; (2) a **copper token currency** that forgers copied, forcing a costly withdrawal; (3) a **tax rise in the Doab** during famine, which drove peasants to flee; and (4) abandoned **Khurasan** and **Qarachil (Himalayan)** expeditions. The traveller **Ibn Battuta** served as his judge (*qazi*).
- **Firoz Shah Tughlaq (1351–1388)** was the welfare king. He dug irrigation **canals**, founded **Firozabad, Hissar, Jaunpur and Fatehabad**, and set up welfare bodies — the **Dar-ul-Shafa** (free hospital), **Diwan-i-Khairat** (marriage help for poor girls) and an employment bureau. He collected four taxes (**Kharaj, Khams, Jizya, Zakat**), imposed **jizya on Brahmins** for the first time, wrote his memoir **Futuhat-i-Firoz Shahi**, and brought two **Ashokan pillars** to Delhi. But he weakened the centre by letting nobles keep iqtas as hereditary.
- **Decline:** after Firoz, weak rulers followed, and **Timur** of Samarqand **sacked Delhi in 1398**; the dynasty ended in **1414**.

**Why it matters:** This is the classic Mains case study of good intentions ruined by poor planning (Muhammad-bin-Tughlaq) versus kindly rule that still weakened the state (Firoz Shah).

**Picture it**

| Ruler | Known for |
|---|---|
| Ghiyasuddin | Tughlaqabad Fort, strong administration |
| Muhammad-bin-Tughlaq | Daulatabad move, token coin, Doab tax, Khurasan/Qarachil |
| Firoz Shah | Canals, welfare bodies, jizya on Brahmins, Ashokan pillars |

**Terms explained**
- **Qarachil** = a Himalayan region targeted by a doomed military expedition.
- **Futuhat-i-Firoz Shahi** = Firoz Shah's own written account of his reign.

**Don't confuse:** The **token currency** is **Muhammad-bin-Tughlaq's** (copper for silver value), not a Khalji reform. **Tughlaqabad** was built by **Ghiyasuddin**, while **Firoz Shah Kotla** was built by Firoz Shah.

**Remember it:** "MBT = sound ideas, failed execution; Firoz = kind king, weak centre."

**TL;DR**
- Ghiyasuddin founded the dynasty (1320) and built Tughlaqabad Fort.
- Muhammad-bin-Tughlaq's four failed experiments: Daulatabad transfer, token currency, Doab tax rise, Khurasan/Qarachil schemes.
- Firoz Shah built canals, towns and welfare bodies, imposed jizya on Brahmins, wrote Futuhat-i-Firoz Shahi.
- Timur sacked Delhi (1398); the Tughlaq dynasty ended in 1414.
keyPoints: Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq founded the dynasty in 1320 and built Tughlaqabad Fort.
Muhammad-bin-Tughlaq's experiments: Daulatabad capital transfer, copper token currency, Doab tax rise, Khurasan/Qarachil schemes — all failed.
Firoz Shah Tughlaq built canals, towns and welfare institutions and imposed jizya on Brahmins.
Firoz Shah wrote Futuhat-i-Firoz Shahi and brought two Ashokan pillars to Delhi.
Timur sacked Delhi in 1398; the Tughlaq dynasty ended in 1414, replaced by the Sayyids.

items.title: Sayyid & Lodi Dynasties — the Final Phase
items.body:
### The Sayyid & Lodi Dynasties, 1414–1526

**In one line:** The last two dynasties of a shrunken Sultanate — the Sayyids who first ruled in Timur's name, and the Lodis, the first Afghan dynasty, whose last king lost to Babur in 1526.

**Why it is asked:** The founders, the odd title 'Rayat-i-Ala', the founding of Agra and the end at Panipat are the common test points. Define once: *Rayat-i-Ala* = 'exalted banner', a modest title (not 'Sultan') used because the ruler accepted a higher overlord; *Afghan/Pashtun* = an ethnic group from the Afghanistan–north-west frontier region.

**The story**

- The **Sayyid dynasty (1414–1451)** was founded by **Khizr Khan**, who had been **Timur's governor of Multan**. He did not call himself Sultan but took the humble title **Rayat-i-Ala** and ruled in **Timur's name**. The Sayyids claimed descent from the **Prophet Muhammad** to look legitimate. Later, **Mubarak Shah** dropped the nominal allegiance to Timur. The last Sayyid, **Alam Shah**, was pushed aside by **Bahlol Lodi** in **1451**.
- The **Lodi dynasty (1451–1526)** was the **first Afghan (Pashtun)** dynasty of Delhi. **Bahlol Lodi (1451–1489)**, the founder, steadied the kingdom. **Sikandar Lodi (1489–1517)** founded the city of **Agra (1504)**, shifted his administrative focus there and tightened administration. **Ibrahim Lodi (1517–1526)**, the last Sultan, was defeated and killed by **Babur** at the **First Battle of Panipat (1526)** — ending the Sultanate.

**Why it matters:** This phase explains the political weakness and division that let an outsider, Babur, take Delhi so quickly — the bridge from the Sultanate to the Mughals.

**Picture it**

| Ruler | Reign | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Bahlol Lodi | 1451–1489 | Founder; Afghan; consolidated Delhi |
| Sikandar Lodi | 1489–1517 | Founded Agra (1504); centralised rule |
| Ibrahim Lodi | 1517–1526 | Last Sultan; killed by Babur at Panipat |

**Terms explained**
- **Sayyid** = a title claiming descent from the Prophet Muhammad; the dynasty used it for prestige.
- **Lodi Gardens** = the Delhi park where octagonal Lodi-era tombs still stand.

**Don't confuse:** **Bahlol** was the **founder** of the Lodis; **Ibrahim** was the **last** (not first) Lodi ruler. **Agra** was founded by **Sikandar Lodi**, not Babur.

**Remember it:** "Sayyids rule for Timur; Lodis are the first Afghans; Ibrahim falls at Panipat."

**TL;DR**
- Khizr Khan founded the Sayyid dynasty (1414), used the title Rayat-i-Ala, ruled in Timur's name.
- Sayyids claimed descent from the Prophet; Mubarak Shah dropped allegiance to Timur.
- Bahlol Lodi founded the first Afghan dynasty (1451); Sikandar Lodi founded Agra (1504).
- Ibrahim Lodi, the last Sultan, lost to Babur at the First Battle of Panipat (1526).
keyPoints: Khizr Khan founded the Sayyid dynasty in 1414, used the title Rayat-i-Ala and ruled in Timur's name.
Sayyid rulers claimed descent from the Prophet Muhammad; Mubarak Shah asserted independence from Timur.
Bahlol Lodi founded the Lodi dynasty in 1451 — the first Afghan (Pashtun) dynasty of Delhi.
Sikandar Lodi founded the city of Agra (1504) and centralised the administration.
Ibrahim Lodi, the last Sultan, was defeated by Babur at the First Battle of Panipat (1526).

items.title: Administration, Iqta, Architecture & Sources
items.body:
### How the Sultanate was run, built and recorded

**In one line:** The Sultanate held its provinces together through the iqta system, created a new Indo-Islamic style of building, and is known to us through Persian court chronicles.

**Why it is asked:** The meaning of the *iqta*, the 'first true dome', and the main book-and-author pairs are reliable Prelims points. Define once: *iqta* = the right to collect the land tax of an assigned area in return for maintaining soldiers; it was **not** owned land that could be inherited.

**The story**

- **Administration:** the **iqta** linked the provinces to the centre. A noble (an **iqtadar** or **muqti**) was given the tax income of an area and had to keep troops ready for the Sultan with it. Because it was **not hereditary**, the Sultan could move or remove nobles — this broke older feudal habits. Key departments were the **Diwan-i-Wizarat** (finance), **Diwan-i-Arz** (military) and **Diwan-i-Insha** (royal correspondence).
- **Architecture:** the Turks brought the **true arch and the true dome**, minarets and the use of lime mortar — together called the **Indo-Islamic** style. Landmarks include the **Qutub Minar** (begun by Aibak, completed by Iltutmish), the **Alai Darwaza** (Alauddin Khalji, 1311 — the first true dome and arch in India), **Tughlaqabad Fort** (Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq), **Firoz Shah Kotla** (Firoz Shah Tughlaq), and the octagonal tombs of the Lodi rulers in the **Lodi Gardens**.
- **Sources:** most of what we know comes from Persian chronicles written at or near the court.

**Why it matters:** The iqta is the engine of Sultanate administration (a common Mains theme), and Indo-Islamic architecture is a frequent art-and-culture question.

**Picture it**

| Work | Author |
|---|---|
| Tabaqat-i-Nasiri | Minhaj-us-Siraj |
| Taj-ul-Maasir | Hasan Nizami |
| Khazain-ul-Futuh | Amir Khusrau |
| Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi | Ziauddin Barani |
| Rihla (Travels) | Ibn Battuta |

**Terms explained**
- **True arch / true dome** = a curved structure that carries weight by itself using wedge-shaped stones; earlier Indian builders used flat beams instead.
- **Muqti / iqtadar** = the noble who held an iqta and kept soldiers from its revenue.

**Don't confuse:** The **iqta was not private, inheritable land** — it was a revenue assignment the Sultan could take back. **Qutub Minar** was *begun* by Aibak but *completed* by Iltutmish.

**Remember it:** "Iqta = pay-with-tax-for-troops, on loan from the Sultan — never owned."

**TL;DR**
- The iqta was a non-hereditary revenue assignment to nobles (muqtis) who maintained troops.
- Indo-Islamic style brought the true arch and dome; the Alai Darwaza (1311) was the first true dome/arch in India.
- Qutub Minar: begun by Aibak, completed by Iltutmish; Lodi Gardens preserve octagonal tombs.
- Key books: Barani (Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi), Amir Khusrau (Khazain-ul-Futuh), Minhaj (Tabaqat-i-Nasiri), Ibn Battuta (Rihla).
keyPoints: The iqta was a non-hereditary revenue assignment to nobles (muqtis) who maintained troops — the backbone of Sultanate administration.
Indo-Islamic architecture introduced the true arch and dome; the Alai Darwaza (1311) was the first true dome/arch in India.
Qutub Minar was begun by Aibak and completed by Iltutmish; Lodi Gardens preserve octagonal Sultanate tombs.
Amir Khusrau ('Parrot of India') wrote Khazain-ul-Futuh; Ziauddin Barani wrote Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi.
Ibn Battuta's Rihla describes India under Muhammad-bin-Tughlaq; Minhaj-us-Siraj wrote Tabaqat-i-Nasiri.

items.title: Before the Sultanate — Arabs, Ghaznavids and Ghurids
items.body:
### Before the Sultanate — Arabs, Ghaznavids and Ghurids

**In one line**
Three waves came before 1206: the Arabs in Sindh (712), the raids of Mahmud of Ghazni (1000–1027), and the conquests of Muhammad Ghori that founded Turkish rule.

**The story**
In **712** **Muhammad bin Qasim** took Sindh from **Dahir**; the story is told in the **Chachnama**, and the Pratiharas, **Bappa Rawal** and the Chalukyas stopped further Arab advance. In Afghanistan **Sabuktigin** built the Ghaznavid state, and his son **Mahmud** made **17** raids into India. **Alberuni** and **Firdausi** worked at his court, and **Utbi** wrote its history. The Ghurid **Muhammad Ghori** came through the **Gomal** Pass, took **Multan** and **Lahore**, fought Prithviraj over **Bhatinda**, and won at Tarain (1192) through superior **cavalry**. His general **Bakhtiyar Khalji** destroyed **Nalanda** and surprised **Lakshmana Sena** at **Nadia**. Ghori was killed by the **Khokhars** in 1206, and his slaves — Aibak, **Yalduz** and **Qubacha** — fought over his empire.

#### The Arabs and the Ghaznavids

| Person / work | Date | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| **Muhammad bin Qasim** | **712** CE | Conquered Sindh for the Umayyads; nephew and son-in-law of Hajjaj, governor of Iraq |
| **Dahir** | 712 | King of Sindh; lost the port **Debal** and then his life to Qasim |
| **Chachnama** | 13th c. Persian | History of the Arab conquest of Sindh (Persian translation by Ali Kufi) |
| **Arabs checked** | 8th c. | By the Pratihara Nagabhata I, **Bappa Rawal** (Kalbhoja) of Mewar and the Chalukyas of the Deccan |
| **Sabuktigin** | 977–997 | Real founder of the Ghaznavid state; defeated the Hindushahi Jayapala |
| **Mahmud of Ghazni** | 998–1030 | **17** raids (1000–1027): Waihind (Anandapala, 1008–09), Kannauj (1018), Somnath (1025) |
| **Alberuni** | 973–1048 | Scholar in Mahmud's train; wrote the **Kitab-ul-Hind** (Tahqiq-i-Hind) on Indian society and science |
| **Firdausi** | c.1010 | Wrote the Persian epic **Shahnama** at Mahmud's court |
| **Utbi** | — | **Tarikh-i-Yamini** — court history of Mahmud (Yamin-ud-Daula) |

#### Muhammad Ghori and his generals

| Event | Fact |
|---|---|
| **1173–1175** | Ghori took Ghazni (1173); came via the **Gomal** Pass; took **Multan** and Uch (1175) |
| **1186** | Took **Lahore** from the last Ghaznavid, Khusrau Malik |
| **Bhatinda** (Tabarhind) | The fort whose seizure by Ghori started the clash with Prithviraj (1191) |
| **Why Tarain II was lost** | Superior Turkish **cavalry** (mounted archers), speed and organisation; Rajput disunity |
| **Nadia** (c.1204) | Bakhtiyar Khalji surprised **Lakshmana Sena** at Nadia; Lakhnauti became the Turkish base in Bengal |
| **Monasteries destroyed** | **Bakhtiyar** Khalji sacked **Nalanda**, Vikramshila and Odantapuri |
| **Andkhud** (1204) | Defeat by the **Khwarizm** Shah ended Ghurid hopes in Central Asia (the PDF gives 1203) |
| **Death (1206)** | Killed at Damyak (Jhelum) by the **Khokhar**s; his Indian conquests passed to Aibak |
| **Heirs** | Aibak (Delhi/Lahore), **Yalduz** (Ghazni), **Qubacha** (Multan and Sindh) |

**Don't confuse**
- **Mahmud of Ghazni** (raids, 1000–1027, no empire in India) ≠ **Muhammad Ghori** (conquest, 1175–1206, founded Turkish rule). The PDF mixes their names in one place.
- **Alberuni** = Kitab-ul-Hind; **Firdausi** = Shahnama; **Utbi** = Tarikh-i-Yamini.

**TL;DR**
- 712 Qasim beat Dahir (Chachnama).
- Sabuktigin founded Ghaznavid power; Mahmud raided 17 times; Alberuni, Firdausi, Utbi.
- Ghori: Gomal Pass, Multan 1175, Lahore 1186, Bhatinda, Tarain; Bakhtiyar Khalji — Nalanda, Nadia; Ghori killed by the Khokhars (1206).
keyPoints: Muhammad bin Qasim conquered Sindh in 712, defeating Dahir; the Chachnama records it.
Sabuktigin founded Ghaznavid power; Mahmud of Ghazni raided India 17 times (1000–1027).
Alberuni wrote the Kitab-ul-Hind; Firdausi wrote the Shahnama at Mahmud's court.
Ghori entered by the Gomal Pass, took Multan (1175) and Lahore (1186); Turkish cavalry won the Second Battle of Tarain.
Bakhtiyar Khalji destroyed Nalanda and took Nadia from Lakshmana Sena; Ghori was killed by the Khokhars in 1206.

items.title: Slave Dynasty — Iltutmish's Consolidation, Razia's Court and Balban's Kingship
items.body:
### Slave Dynasty — Iltutmish's Consolidation, Razia's Court and Balban's Kingship

**In one line**
Exams go beyond "Lakh Baksh" and the silver tanka to ask how Iltutmish secured the throne (Jud, Yalduz, Mangbarni, the Caliph), what upset the nobles about Razia, and which institutions Balban created.

**The story**
**Iltutmish**, an **Ilbari** Turk, beat **Aram Shah** at **Jud** and **Yalduz** at Tarain (1216). In 1221 he refused shelter to **Mangbarni**, so **Chengiz** Khan turned back, and in **1229** the Abbasid **Caliph** recognised him. He built **Sultan Ghari**, the first Islamic tomb in India. **Razia** angered the Turkish nobles by promoting the **Abyssinian** **Yaqut**. Under **Bahram Shah** the nobles created the **Naib-i-Mamlakat**, and **Nasiruddin Mahmud** lived simply while Balban governed; the **Tabaqat-i-Nasiri** is named after him. As Sultan, **Balban** set up the **Diwan-i-Arz**, brought in **Nauroz**, and lost his heir **Prince Muhammad** to the Mongols. Under **Kaiqubad** the dynasty fell apart.

#### The Slave Sultans in detail

| Ruler / event | Reign / date | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| **Aram Shah** | 1210–1211 | Aibak's successor at Lahore; defeated by Iltutmish at **Jud** near Delhi |
| **Iltutmish** | 1211–1236 | An **Ilbari** Turk, slave and son-in-law of Aibak; the real consolidator of the Sultanate |
| **Third Tarain** (1216) | — | Iltutmish defeated **Yalduz** of Ghazni; Qubacha later drowned in the Indus (1228) |
| **Mongol danger** (1221) | — | Refused shelter to the Khwarizm prince **Mangbarni**, so **Chengiz** Khan turned back from the Indus |
| **Investiture** (1229) | — | The Abbasid **Caliph** al-Mustansir recognised him — legal sovereignty for the Sultanate |
| **Sultan Ghari** | 1231 | **First** Islamic tomb (mausoleum) in India — for his son; he also built the Hauz-i-Shamsi tank |
| **Razia** | 1236–1240 | Wore male dress (qaba and kulah); made the **Abyssinian** Jamaluddin **Yaqut** master of the stables; killed near Kaithal (1240) |
| **Bahram Shah** | 1240–1242 | Nobles created the regent's post **Naib-i-Mamlakat** to control the Sultan |
| **Nasiruddin Mahmud** | 1246–1265 | Copied the Quran for a living; Balban (Ulugh Khan) ran the state; **Tabaqat-i-Nasiri** is named after him |
| **Balban** | 1266–1287 | Created the **Diwan-i-Arz** (military department); introduced the Persian festival Nauroz; kingship as Niyabat-i-Khudai |
| **Nauroz** | — | Persian new-year festival introduced at court by Balban |
| **Prince Muhammad** | d.1285 | Balban's heir and governor of Multan; patron of Amir Khusrau; killed by the Mongols |
| **Kaiqubad** | 1287–1290 | Balban's grandson; built **Kilokhri**; the last Slave ruler was the child Kayumars (1290) |

**Don't confuse**
- **Sultan Ghari** (1231) = first Islamic **tomb**; **Quwwat-ul-Islam** = first mosque at Delhi.
- **Diwan-i-Arz** (Balban) = military; **Diwan-i-Riyasat** (Alauddin) = markets; **Diwan-i-Kohi** (Muhammad bin Tughlaq) = agriculture.
- **Tabaqat-i-Nasiri** is named after **Nasiruddin Mahmud** (Slave dynasty), not Nasiruddin Khusrau Khan.

**TL;DR**
- Iltutmish: Ilbari; Jud (Aram Shah); Tarain 1216 (Yalduz); Mangbarni 1221; Caliph 1229; Sultan Ghari.
- Razia: Yaqut the Abyssinian; Bahram Shah: Naib-i-Mamlakat.
- Nasiruddin Mahmud — Tabaqat-i-Nasiri; Balban — Diwan-i-Arz, Nauroz.
keyPoints: Iltutmish (an Ilbari Turk) beat Aram Shah at Jud and Yalduz at Tarain (1216).
He refused shelter to Mangbarni (1221), keeping Chengiz Khan away, and got investiture from the Abbasid Caliph (1229).
Sultan Ghari, built by Iltutmish for his son, is the first Islamic tomb in India.
Razia promoted the Abyssinian Jamaluddin Yaqut; under Bahram Shah the nobles created the Naib-i-Mamlakat.
Minhaj's Tabaqat-i-Nasiri is named after Nasiruddin Mahmud; Balban set up the Diwan-i-Arz and introduced Nauroz.

items.title: Khaljis — Titles, Campaign Details, Revenue Reforms and Amir Khusrau
items.body:
### Khaljis — Titles, Campaign Details, Revenue Reforms and Amir Khusrau

**In one line**
For the Khaljis the details asked are Alauddin's title, who held Ranthambore and Chittor, Siri fort, the revenue rate and new taxes, Mubarak Shah's claim to be Khalifa, and Amir Khusrau's works.

**The story**
**Jalaluddin** settled Mongol converts — the **New Muslims** — near Delhi. **Alauddin** called himself **Sikandar-i-Sani**. His generals **Ulugh Khan** and **Nusrat Khan** took Gujarat (1299) and captured **Malik Kafur** at **Cambay**. Ranthambore fell with **Hammir** Deva (1301) and Chittor with **Ratan Singh** (1303); the Padmini tale comes from the much later **Padmavat**. Against the **Mongols** he built **Siri**. He took **half** the produce by **measurement**, added **ghari** and **charai**, set up the **Diwan-i-Mustakhraj**, and cut down the **khuts** and **muqaddams**. His son **Mubarak** Shah called himself **Khalifa**, and **Khusrau Khan** ended the line. **Amir Khusrau**, the **Tuti-i-Hind**, wrote for five Sultans.

#### Khalji rulers, campaigns and reforms

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **New Muslims** | Mongols settled near Delhi (Mughalpura) under Jalaluddin after accepting Islam; Alauddin later massacred them |
| **Sikandar-i-Sani** | Alauddin's title — 'the second Alexander'; he also dreamt of founding a new religion |
| **Malik Kafur** | '**Hazardinari**' (bought for 1,000 dinars); captured at **Cambay** by Nusrat Khan in 1299 |
| **Gujarat** (1299) | **Ulugh Khan** and **Nusrat Khan** beat Karna Vaghela; Somnath sacked again |
| **Ranthambore** (1301) | Held by the Chauhan **Hammir** Deva, killed when the fort fell |
| **Chittor** (1303) | Rana **Ratan Singh**; renamed Khizrabad; the Padmini legend is from Jayasi's **Padmavat** (1540), written much later |
| **Siri** (c.1303) | Built during the **Mongol**s' siege of Delhi (Targhi, 1303); the second of the seven cities of Delhi |
| **Land revenue** | **Half** the produce, assessed by **measurement** (masahat) with the biswa as unit |
| **Ghari** and **charai** | House tax and grazing tax on cattle |
| **Diwan-i-Mustakhraj** | Department to recover arrears of revenue from officials and village heads |
| **Intermediaries curbed** | The **khuts**, **muqaddam**s and chaudharis lost their privileges and paid the same taxes |
| **Kafur's campaign dates** | Devagiri 1307–08, Warangal **1309**–10, Dwarasamudra **1311**, Madurai **1311** (the PDF gives conflicting years) |
| **Madurai** (1311) | Exploited the civil war between Vira Pandya and **Sundara Pandya** |
| **Mubarak Shah Khalji** | 1316–1320; the only Sultan to call himself **Khalifa**; undid many of his father's harsh rules |
| **Khusrau Khan** | 1320; a **Baradu** convert from Gujarat; ruled as Nasiruddin until Ghazi Malik killed him |
| **Hauz-i-Alai** & **Alai Minar** | The great tank (later Hauz Khas) and an unfinished minar meant to be twice the Qutb Minar |

#### Amir Khusrau — the court poet of five Sultans

| Work / title | Subject |
|---|---|
| **Tuti-i-Hind** | 'Parrot of India' — Amir Khusrau, disciple of Nizamuddin Auliya; wrote in Persian and Hindavi |
| **Music** | Credited with the **qawwali**; tradition (not proof) links him with the sitar and tabla |
| **Guru** | Disciple of the Chishti saint **Nizamuddin** Auliya; buried near him in Delhi |
| **Qiran-us-Sadain** | Meeting of Kaiqubad and his father Bughra Khan (1289) |
| **Miftah-ul-Futuh** | Jalaluddin Khalji's campaigns |
| **Ashiqa** | Love story of Alauddin's son Khizr Khan and **Deval Rani** of Gujarat |
| **Nuh Sipihr** | 'Nine Skies' — Mubarak Shah's reign and praise of India and Hindavi |
| **Tughlaq Nama** | Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq's rise to power (the PDF wrongly lists it under Alauddin's court) |

**Don't confuse**
- **Ghari** = house tax, **charai** = grazing tax; **jizya** = tax on non-Muslims, **zakat** = tax on Muslims.
- **Diwan-i-Mustakhraj** (arrears, Alauddin) ≠ **Diwan-i-Riyasat** (markets, Alauddin) ≠ **Diwan-i-Kohi** (agriculture, Muhammad bin Tughlaq).
- **Tughlaq Nama** is about **Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq**; **Khazain-ul-Futuh** is about Alauddin's conquests.

**TL;DR**
- Alauddin = Sikandar-i-Sani; Malik Kafur (Hazardinari) taken at Cambay; Hammir (Ranthambore), Ratan Singh (Chittor), Siri fort.
- Revenue: half the produce by measurement; ghari, charai; Diwan-i-Mustakhraj; khuts and muqaddams curbed.
- Mubarak Shah = Khalifa; Khusrau Khan (Baradu).
- Amir Khusrau: Tuti-i-Hind, qawwali, Nizamuddin Auliya; Qiran-us-Sadain, Miftah-ul-Futuh, Ashiqa, Nuh Sipihr, Tughlaq Nama.
keyPoints: Alauddin Khalji took the title Sikandar-i-Sani; Malik Kafur ('Hazardinari') was captured at Cambay in 1299.
Ranthambore (1301) was held by Hammir Deva; Chittor (1303) by Ratan Singh — the Padmini story is from Jayasi's Padmavat (1540).
Siri fort was built against the Mongols; land revenue was half the produce by measurement; ghari (house) and charai (grazing) taxes.
Alauddin set up the Diwan-i-Mustakhraj; Mubarak Shah Khalji was the only Sultan to call himself Khalifa.
Amir Khusrau (Tuti-i-Hind, disciple of Nizamuddin Auliya) wrote the Ashiqa, Nuh Sipihr and Tughlaq Nama.

items.title: Tughlaqs — Founder, Experiments, Firoz's Departments and Timur
items.body:
### Tughlaqs — Founder, Experiments, Firoz's Departments and Timur

**In one line**
Beyond the four experiments of Muhammad bin Tughlaq, exams ask the dates (1327, 1329), the agriculture department and loans, Ibn Battuta's role, Firoz's departments and taxes, and the two books called Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi.

**The story**
**Ghazi Malik**, governor of **Dipalpur**, became **Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq**, dug the first **canals**, and died under a pavilion at **Afghanpur** (1325). His son moved the capital to Daulatabad (**1327**), issued tokens (**1329**), created the **Diwan-i-Kohi** and gave **taccavi** loans, lost an army in **Kumaon**, and built **Jahanpanah**. The **Moroccan** **Ibn Battuta** was his qazi and went as envoy to **China**. **Vijayanagara** and the **Bahmani** kingdom broke away, and he died at **Thatta**. **Firoz** created the **Diwan-i-Bandagan**, kept to the four Sharia taxes, added **haq-i-sharb**, dug a **Yamuna–Hissar** canal and moved the **Topra** pillar. **Afif** and **Barani** both wrote a Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi. **Timur** came in 1398, and the **Sharqi** kingdom rose at Jaunpur.

#### Ghiyasuddin and Muhammad bin Tughlaq

| Item | Date | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| **Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq** | 1320–1325 | Earlier **Ghazi Malik**, governor of **Dipalpur**; policy of moderation (rasm-i-miyana) |
| **Irrigation** | — | Barani calls him the **first Sultan** to dig **canals**; Firoz built many more |
| **Death** (1325) | — | A welcome pavilion at **Afghanpur** collapsed (suspicion falls on his son) |
| **Hunuz Dilli dur ast** | — | 'Delhi is still far' — Nizamuddin Auliya's reply to Ghiyasuddin's threats |
| **Daulatabad** | **1327** | Capital moved from Delhi to Devagiri (renamed Daulatabad); later reversed |
| **Token currency** | **1329**–30 | Bronze/copper tokens at the value of silver; mass forgery forced withdrawal |
| **Diwan-i-Kohi** | — | Department of agriculture to extend cultivation with state loans |
| **Taccavi** | — | State loans to peasants (also called sondhar); Firoz wrote them off |
| **Qarachil** | — | A Himalayan (**Kumaon**) expedition, wiped out by the hills and rains |
| **Khurasan plan** | — | An army of **3,70,000** raised and paid for a year, then disbanded |
| **Ibn Battuta** | 1333–1342 | A **Moroccan**; qazi of Delhi for eight years; sent as envoy to **China**; wrote the Rihla |
| **Jahanpanah** | — | 'Refuge of the World' — the fourth city of Delhi, joining Siri and Qila Rai Pithora; **Bijai Mandal** palace |
| **Death** (1351) | — | Died at **Thatta** chasing the rebel Taghi; Badauni: 'the Sultan was freed of his people and they of him' |
| **Breakaway states** | — | Madurai Sultanate (1335), **Vijayanagara** (1336), Bengal (1338), **Bahmani** (1347) |

#### Firoz Shah Tughlaq

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Diwan-i-Bandagan** | Department of slaves (about 1,80,000 slaves trained in crafts) |
| **Diwan-i-Istihqaq** | Department for pensions and financial aid to the poor |
| **Four Sharia taxes** | Kharaj (land), **khams** (one-fifth of war booty), jizya (non-Muslims), **zakat** (on Muslims) |
| **Haq-i-sharb** | Irrigation tax of one-tenth on canal-watered land |
| **Canals** | From the **Yamuna** to **Hissar**, and from the Sutlej to the Ghaggar — forerunners of the Western Yamuna canal |
| **Ashokan pillars** | From **Topra** (Ambala) to Firoz Shah Kotla, and from **Meerut** to the Ridge |
| **Dalail-i-Firoz Shahi** | Persian translation of Sanskrit texts taken from the Jwalamukhi temple at Nagarkot |
| **Shams-i-Siraj Afif** | His own **Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi** on Firoz's reign — different from Barani's book of the same name |
| **Barani** | **Fatawa-i-Jahandari** (political ideas) and Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi (Balban to Firoz) |
| **Jajnagar campaign** | Raided Odisha and desecrated the Jagannath temple at **Puri**; two failed Bengal campaigns (1353, 1359) |
| **Towns** | Firozabad (the fifth city of Delhi), Hissar, Jaunpur, **Fatehabad** |
| **Qutb Minar repair** | Rebuilt the top storeys after **lightning** (1368), adding marble |

#### Later Tughlaqs and Timur

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Timur** (1398) | Invaded in the reign of **Nasiruddin Mahmud Shah** Tughlaq (the PDF also names Nasiruddin Muhammad) |
| **Timur** | Ruler of Samarqand; memoir **Malfuzat-i-Timuri**; left Khizr Khan as governor of Multan |
| **Sharqi kingdom** | **Jaunpur**, founded 1394 by Malik Sarwar (Malik-us-Sharq); conquered by Bahlol Lodi |

**Don't confuse**
- Two **Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi**: **Barani** (Balban to early Firoz) and **Shams-i-Siraj Afif** (Firoz's reign). Firoz's own memoir is the **Futuhat-i-Firoz Shahi**.
- **Diwan-i-Kohi** (agriculture, Muhammad bin Tughlaq) ≠ **Diwan-i-Bandagan** (slaves, Firoz) ≠ **Diwan-i-Istihqaq** (pensions, Firoz).
- **Ibn Battuta** (Moroccan, Tughlaq) ≠ **Alberuni** (Khwarizm, Mahmud of Ghazni).

**TL;DR**
- Ghazi Malik (Dipalpur) → first canals → Afghanpur 1325; Hunuz Dilli dur ast.
- MBT: Daulatabad 1327; tokens 1329; Diwan-i-Kohi; taccavi; Qarachil (Kumaon); Jahanpanah; Thatta 1351.
- Firoz: Diwan-i-Bandagan, Istihqaq; four Sharia taxes; haq-i-sharb; Yamuna–Hissar canal; Topra pillar; Dalail-i-Firoz Shahi.
- Timur 1398 (Malfuzat-i-Timuri); Sharqi Jaunpur 1394.
keyPoints: Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq (Ghazi Malik, governor of Dipalpur) died at Afghanpur in 1325.
Muhammad bin Tughlaq moved the capital to Daulatabad in 1327, created the Diwan-i-Kohi and gave taccavi loans; Jahanpanah was the fourth city of Delhi.
Ibn Battuta, a Moroccan, was qazi of Delhi and was sent as envoy to China.
Firoz Shah created the Diwan-i-Bandagan (slaves); levied haq-i-sharb; brought the Topra and Meerut pillars to Delhi.
Shams-i-Siraj Afif and Ziauddin Barani each wrote a Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi; Barani also wrote the Fatawa-i-Jahandari.

items.title: Sayyids & Lodis — Coins, Measures, Tombs and the Road to Panipat
items.body:
### Sayyids & Lodis — Coins, Measures, Tombs and the Road to Panipat

**In one line**
The last two dynasties are tested on a few distinctive items: the Tarikh-i-Mubarak Shahi, the Bahloli coin, Sikandar's pen-name and measuring yard, the first garden tomb, and who invited Babur.

**The story**
**Mubarak Shah** Sayyid is remembered through **Sirhindi**'s **Tarikh-i-Mubarak Shahi**; **Muhammad Shah**'s **octagonal** tomb stands in the Lodi Gardens, and **Alam Shah** retired to **Badaun**. **Bahlol** Lodi founded the **first Afghan** dynasty, issued the **Bahloli** and annexed the **Sharqi** kingdom. **Sikandar** — pen-name **Gulrukhi** — founded Agra and introduced the **Gaz-i-Sikandari**; his tomb is the first **garden tomb**, with a **double dome**. **Ibrahim** lost to **Rana Sanga** at **Khatoli**, and **Daulat Khan** Lodi invited Babur. At Panipat on **21 April** 1526 Ibrahim became the only Sultan killed on the **battlefield**.

#### Sayyids and Lodis in detail

| Ruler / item | Reign | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| **Mubarak Shah** | 1421–1434 | Dropped allegiance to Timur; first to appoint Hindu nobles; **Sirhindi** wrote the **Tarikh-i-Mubarak Shahi** |
| **Muhammad Shah** | 1434–1443 | His **octagonal** tomb is in the Lodi Gardens |
| **Alam Shah** | 1443–1451 | Retired to **Badaun**; Bahlol Lodi took Delhi |
| **Bahlol Lodi** | 1451–1489 | Issued the copper **Bahloli** coin (used till Akbar); sat with nobles as an equal; annexed the Sharqi kingdom of Jaunpur |
| **Jaunpur annexed** | — | **Bahlol** defeated Husain Shah **Sharqi** and annexed Jaunpur (c.1484) |
| **Sikandar Lodi** | 1489–1517 | Pen-name **Gulrukhi**; founded Agra (1504); Gaz-i-Sikandari; abolished grain duties |
| **Gaz-i-Sikandari** | — | A standard yard of 39 digits (about 30 inches) for measuring land |
| **Sikandar Lodi's tomb** | — | First enclosed **garden tomb** in India; an early **double dome** |
| **Ibrahim Lodi** | 1517–1526 | Lost to **Rana Sanga** at **Khatoli**; his harshness drove Daulat Khan Lodi to invite Babur |
| **Invitation to Babur** | — | **Daulat Khan** Lodi (Punjab) and Alam Khan (Ibrahim's uncle) invited Babur |
| **Panipat** (**21 April** 1526) | — | Ibrahim was the only Sultan to die on the **battlefield**; Babur used tulughma and artillery |
| **Ethnic shift** | — | The Lodis were the **first Afghan** (Pashtun) rulers; earlier dynasties were Turkish |

**Don't confuse**
- **Bahloli** = copper coin (Bahlol Lodi); **tanka** = silver coin (Iltutmish); **jital** = copper coin (Iltutmish).
- **Gaz-i-Sikandari** (Sikandar Lodi) is a measuring yard; **Sikandar-i-Sani** (Alauddin Khalji) is a title.

**TL;DR**
- Sirhindi — Tarikh-i-Mubarak Shahi; Alam Shah to Badaun.
- Bahlol: Bahloli coin, Jaunpur annexed; first Afghan dynasty.
- Sikandar: Gulrukhi, Agra 1504, Gaz-i-Sikandari, garden tomb with a double dome.
- Ibrahim: Khatoli (Rana Sanga); Daulat Khan invited Babur; killed at Panipat, 21 April 1526.
keyPoints: Yahya Sirhindi's Tarikh-i-Mubarak Shahi covers the Sayyids; Alam Shah retired to Badaun (1451).
Bahlol Lodi issued the Bahloli copper coin and annexed the Sharqi kingdom; the Lodis were the first Afghan dynasty.
Sikandar Lodi wrote as 'Gulrukhi' and introduced the Gaz-i-Sikandari; his tomb is the first garden tomb with a double dome.
Ibrahim Lodi lost to Rana Sanga at Khatoli; Daulat Khan Lodi invited Babur.
Ibrahim Lodi was the only Delhi Sultan to die on the battlefield (Panipat, 21 April 1526).

items.title: Sultanate Administration, Taxes, Coins, Architecture & Chroniclers — the Full Set
items.body:
### Sultanate Administration, Taxes, Coins, Architecture & Chroniclers — the Full Set

**In one line**
This note gathers the central departments, the units below the province, the taxes and coins, the building milestones and the chroniclers — the term-to-meaning pairs that fill match-the-following questions.

**The story**
At the centre the **wazir** ran the **Diwan-i-Wizarat**, the **dabir** the **Diwan-i-Insha**, the **sadr** the **Diwan-i-Risalat**, and the **qazi-ul-quzat** the courts; the **barid-i-mamalik** ran intelligence. Below the iqta came the **shiq** and the **pargana**; in the village the **muqaddam** and **patwari** served. **Khalisa** land paid straight to the treasury, and the iqta was the forerunner of the Mughal **jagir**. Taxes included **zakat**, jizya and **khams**; the tanka weighed **175** grains. In building, the **Quwwat-ul-Islam** came first, **Balban**'s tomb has the **first true arch**, the Qutb Minar (**five storeys**) is a UNESCO site since **1993**, Tughlaq walls are **sloping** and Lodi tombs **octagonal**. Delhi grew as **seven cities**. Chroniclers include **Hasan Nizami**, **Isami**, Firoz himself, Amir Khusrau and Ibn Battuta.

#### Central and local administration

| Office / term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Diwan-i-Wizarat** | Finance and revenue — headed by the **wazir** (prime minister) |
| **Diwan-i-Insha** | Royal correspondence — headed by the **dabir**-i-mamalik |
| **Diwan-i-Risalat** | Religious affairs and grants — headed by the **sadr**-us-sudur |
| **Diwan-i-Qaza** | Justice — headed by the chief judge **qazi-ul-quzat** |
| **Barid-i-mamalik** | Head of intelligence and the news-reporting system |
| **Mustaufi** / **mushrif**-i-mamalik | Auditor-general / accountant-general under the wazir |
| **Shiq** → **pargana** → village | District (shiq, under a shiqdar) → pargana (group of villages, under an amil) |
| **Village officials** | **Muqaddam** (headman), chaudhari, **patwari** (record-keeper) |
| **Khalisa** | Crown land; its revenue went straight to the Sultan's treasury |
| **Iqta vs jagir** | The Sultanate **iqta** was the forerunner of the Mughal **jagir**; both were revenue assignments, not hereditary |
| **Zakat** | Tax on Muslims, about **2.5**% of wealth; **jizya** on non-Muslims |
| **Khams** | State share of war booty — **one-fifth** by Sharia; Alauddin and Muhammad bin Tughlaq took four-fifths |
| **Tanka** | Silver coin of about **175** grains (Iltutmish); 48 jitals to a tanka |

#### Architecture milestones

| Monument / style | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Quwwat-ul-Islam** | First mosque at Delhi; built from the remains of **27** temples; begun by Aibak |
| **Qutb Minar complex** | UNESCO site **1993**; minar ~72.5 m, five storeys of red and buff sandstone |
| **Qutb Minar** | **Five storeys**, about **72.5** m: Aibak built the base, Iltutmish added three, Firoz rebuilt the top |
| **Balban's tomb** | Mehrauli; the **first true arch** in India (the Alai Darwaza, 1311, has the first true dome) |
| **Tughlaq style** | **Sloping** (battered) walls, grey stone; Ghiyasuddin's tomb at Tughlaqabad is the model |
| **Lodi style** | **Octagonal** (for rulers) and square tombs, double domes; Bara Gumbad and Moth ki Masjid |
| **Seven cities of Delhi** | Qila Rai Pithora, Siri, Tughlaqabad, Jahanpanah, Firozabad, **Dinpanah** (Purana Qila), Shahjahanabad |

#### Chroniclers and their works

| Author | Work |
|---|---|
| **Hasan Nizami** | **Taj-ul-Maasir** — reign of Qutb-ud-din Aibak |
| **Isami** | **Futuh-us-Salatin** — verse history of the Sultans, written under the Bahmanis; critical of Muhammad bin Tughlaq |
| **Firoz Shah** | **Futuhat-i-Firoz Shahi** — his own record of his reign |
| **Amir Khusrau** | **Khazain-ul-Futuh** — Alauddin's conquests (including the Deccan) |
| **Ibn Battuta** | **Rihla** — travels, including Muhammad bin Tughlaq's court |

**Don't confuse**
- **Iqta** (Sultanate) → **jagir** (Mughal) → **nayankara** (Vijayanagara/Kakatiya): three systems of revenue assignment for military service; do not swap the names.
- **First true arch** = Balban's tomb; **first true dome** = Alai Darwaza (1311). Some books credit both to the Alai Darwaza.
- **Diwan-i-Insha** = correspondence; **Diwan-i-Risalat** = religious affairs.

**TL;DR**
- Wazir — Wizarat; dabir — Insha; sadr — Risalat; qazi-ul-quzat — Qaza; barid-i-mamalik — intelligence.
- Shiq → pargana → village (muqaddam, patwari); khalisa = crown land; iqta → jagir.
- Zakat 2.5%; khams 1/5; tanka 175 grains.
- Quwwat-ul-Islam (27 temples); Balban's tomb (first arch); Qutb UNESCO 1993; seven cities of Delhi.
- Hasan Nizami, Isami, Futuhat-i-Firoz Shahi, Khazain-ul-Futuh, Rihla.
keyPoints: Diwan-i-Wizarat (wazir), Diwan-i-Insha (dabir), Diwan-i-Risalat (sadr-us-sudur), Diwan-i-Qaza (qazi-ul-quzat); barid-i-mamalik headed intelligence.
Provinces → shiqs (shiqdar) → parganas; khalisa was crown land; the iqta was the forerunner of the Mughal jagir.
Zakat (2.5%) on Muslims, jizya on non-Muslims, khams (one-fifth of booty); the tanka weighed about 175 grains.
Quwwat-ul-Islam used material from 27 temples; Balban's tomb has the first true arch; the Qutb complex is a UNESCO site (1993).
Hasan Nizami — Taj-ul-Maasir; Isami — Futuh-us-Salatin; Firoz — Futuhat-i-Firoz Shahi; Khusrau — Khazain-ul-Futuh; Ibn Battuta — Rihla.

items.title: For Mains — The Delhi Sultanate
items.body:
## For Mains — The Delhi Sultanate (Paper-II, clause M2-2)

Mains rarely asks "who/when"; it asks you to **analyse** the Sultanate as a state — its institutions, its reforms, and why it both lasted 300 years and ultimately fell. Build answers around these dimensions.

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Nature of the state | A centralised, military, Persianised monarchy resting on the iqta and a slave/noble elite; theory of kingship (Balban's Zill-i-Ilahi). |
| Administrative innovation | Iqta system, the three central diwans, Alauddin's price control and Dagh–Chehra army. |
| Economy & society | Monetisation (silver tanka), urban growth, new crafts, agrarian taxation (kharaj), the ulema vs the Sultan. |
| Culture | Indo-Islamic architecture (true arch/dome), Persian chronicles, Amir Khusrau, the beginnings of a composite culture and Bhakti–Sufi contact. |
| Why it declined | Over-centralisation, succession wars, over-mighty nobles (hereditary iqtas under Firoz), Timur's invasion (1398), provincial breakaways. |
| AP / Deccan angle | Malik Kafur's raids (1309–1311) shattered the Kakatiyas of Warangal and the Yadavas, indirectly clearing the ground for Vijayanagara and the Bahmani kingdom. |

**Data points and authorities to quote:** Alauddin's three markets (mandi, Sarai Adl, horse-market) and the Diwan-i-Riyasat; Dagh (horse-branding) and Chehra (soldier roll); the silver tanka of Iltutmish; Ziauddin Barani's *Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi* and Ibn Battuta's *Rihla* as primary sources; the Alai Darwaza (1311) as the first true dome in India; Timur's sack of Delhi (1398).

**Use in answers:**
- *Example:* contrast Alauddin's enforced price control (worked briefly through fear) with Muhammad-bin-Tughlaq's token currency (failed through poor execution) to argue that Sultanate reforms depended on the ruler, not on institutions.
- *Quote:* Barani's judgement that Muhammad-bin-Tughlaq's schemes were sound in conception but ruinous in execution.
- *Diagram idea:* a timeline bar (1206–1526) with the five dynasties and three turning points (1192 Tarain II, 1311 Alai Darwaza, 1398 Timur) to frame rise–peak–decline.
- *AP link:* use Malik Kafur's Deccan raids to connect this topic to the Vijayanagara–Bahmani answer in the same paper.
keyPoints: Frame the Sultanate as a centralised military-Persianate state built on the iqta and a theory of kingship (Zill-i-Ilahi).
Key institutions/reforms to cite: iqta, central diwans, Alauddin's price control, Dagh–Chehra army, silver tanka.
Decline = over-centralisation + succession wars + hereditary iqtas + Timur's 1398 invasion + provincial breakaways.
AP angle: Malik Kafur's raids (1309–1311) broke the Kakatiyas and Yadavas, opening the way to Vijayanagara and the Bahmanis.
Primary sources to quote: Barani's Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi and Ibn Battuta's Rihla; Alai Darwaza (1311) as the first true dome.
